book: 006 - Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box

chapters.relation: The Rucks argue that Herbert Spencer's Social Darwinism supplied the ideological justification for baseball's color line — blacks were deemed genetically unfit for the game — and that the Negro Leagues disproved it. Rube Foster's Negro National League, and especially Pittsburgh's Homestead Grays and Pittsburgh Crawfords (Cum Posey, Josh Gibson, Satchel Paige, Cool Papa Bell), displayed black organizational skill and on-field excellence, with Negro League teams beating white major leaguers in barnstorming play. Drawing on Darwin's actual account of cultural evolution and Franz Boas's environmental anthropology, the chapter holds that institutions, training infrastructure, and environment — not genes — explain athletic success, as Jackie Robinson's 1947 crossing of the color line and the later rise of Latin stars like Roberto Clemente confirm.

McDaniels reads the Negro Leagues through Nietzsche's account of resentment as revolt and Cornel West's tragic philosophy of resistance: excluded from the white majors after Cap Anson's 1887 stand against George Stovey, black players converted resentment into counter-narratives of excellence, with Satchel Paige, Josh Gibson, and Buck O'Neil showboating and clowning in the tradition of plantation dance, gallows humor, and the blues. The call-and-response sermon scene from The Bingo Long Traveling All-Stars & Motor Kings — Bingo Long on the mound answered by the crowd like a black church congregation — shows performance as ritual that sustains community, while bell hooks's 'absence of presence' frames remembering as resistance to hegemonic definitions of race. The chapter closes with the author's grandfather, for whom Robinson, Aaron, Mays, and Paige proved with every pitch 'We're American Too.'

chapters.file: ch27 - Seventh Inning - The Japanese National Pastime.md
ch28 - Ballparks, Dojos, and Other Places of Enlightenment.md
chapters.relation: Bassham argues that the core advice of hitting instructors like Ted Williams ('get a good ball to hit') and Charley Lau ('tension is the enemy') echoes Zen Buddhist principles, walking through patience, relaxation, self-knowledge, visualization (Reggie Jackson, Willie Stargell, Barry Bonds's on-deck imagery), practice, Bruce Lee-style kime concentration, and mushin or no-mind. Mickey Mantle going 0-for-30 after over-thinking Ted Williams's hitting tips, and Tony Gwynn's 'see the ball and react,' show how conscious analysis interferes with the muscle memory a half-second fastball demands. If kendo is practiced in a dojo — a 'place of enlightenment' — he concludes, ballparks and batting cages may be dojos too, with the caveat that Cobb, Ruth, and Mantle hardly model egoless humility.

Brannigan uses Japanese baseball to ask what is wrong with cultural generalization. He presents the Bushido case — samurai-style self-denial, absolute loyalty (Kawakami's Yomiuri Giants), Suisha Tobita's 'training of death,' resolve (konjo), team harmony (wa), and a relational self grounded in Buddhism's no-self and Confucian identity-through-relationships — then tests it against counter-evidence: Sadaharu Oh's flamingo swing owed as much to individual talent and Hiroshi Arakawa's unconventional kendo-and-aikido coaching as to sensei imitation, the 'new breed' (Ochiai, Egawa) flouts the old ways, and William Kelly's 'Whiting problem' warns against polarizing Japanese and American baseball. The chapter's 'three strikes' against the label 'Japanese baseball' conclude that generalizations become dangerous when treated as monolithic nets cast over an entire culture.

chapters.file: ch30 - Eighth Inning - Behind in the Count.md

chapters.relation: Bennett and Martin argue that the statistics baseball fans treat as objective truth embody far more chance and convention than fans realize. Statistical theory shows luck explains roughly half the spread in 2002 batting averages (Bonds's .370 versus Larry Walker; the 2003 Ramirez–Mueller race decided by one at bat), and Jim Albert's simulation of 1,000 seasons shows about four of five World Series are not won by the most talented team. Drawing on Thomas Kuhn's history of scientific quantification and Theodore Porter's Foucauldian point that numbers 'have agency' and exercise power, they show statistics also act on the game — shaping drafting, salaries, and Hall of Fame election — so Schroeder's stats to Charlie Brown are both indispensable and misleading.

chapters.file: ch32 - Softball The Good Is the Enemy of the Best.md
chapters.relation: Heaphy asks whether softball limits women's potential to be equals on the baseball diamond, using feminist philosophy to explain why women are steered to the 'soft' game. Judith Williamson's analysis of women in mass culture and Simone de Beauvoir's woman-as-invisible-Other explain why female players — the AAGPBL's skirts and charm school, Toni Stone and Mamie Johnson in the Negro Leagues, Ila Borders in the minors — are covered as women first and ballplayers second. Iris Marion Young's 'Throwing Like a Girl' supplies the phenomenology: women throw differently not from anatomy but from experiencing the body as a burden, a socially produced self-fulfilling prophecy. Softball, 'the good,' becomes the enemy of the best — women playing hardball — by letting society postpone hard questions about gender.

chapters.file: ch34 - The Moral and Aesthetic Superiority of Baseball.md
chapters.relation: Kretchmar asks whether the intentional walk of sluggers like Barry Bonds (or Casey at the Bat) is an unfair cop-out. Building an account of games as 'artificial tests' (via Bernard Suits and John Searle's treatment of conventions like 'hello'), he tests the analogy with basketball stalling and finds it fails: walking Bonds shifts rather than avoids the defensive test (the fielding team still owes all its outs), team games legitimately run away from stars as basketball double-teams Shaq, and fans gain new drama — Jeff Kent batting with the tying run after Bonds's walk. He concludes that event-regulated games like baseball, which cannot be shortened, enjoy a moral and aesthetic superiority over time-regulated games, whose endings breed stalling and clock-killing fouls.

Reid argues that baseball and Socratic elenchus are both constructed to cultivate aretē, excellence. She maps four parallels onto concrete moments: both live off uncertainty (pre-game jitters, the 2001 Rivera–Gonzalez Series finish), both require risking failure (Ted Williams playing a doubleheader to protect his .400, Kirk Gibson's hobbling 1988 homer off Dennis Eckersley, Billy Beane's fear beside Lenny Dykstra), both demand active self-testing (Lou Gehrig retiring when complimented on a routine play), and both impose an obligation to return and challenge others — Plato's cave allegory, Socrates the gadfly, the aging champion who applauds the record-breaker. The Delphic oracle's riddle, that Socrates is wisest in knowing his ignorance, is the batter's-box humility every at-bat demands.

A paired debate on whether Pete Rose belongs in the Hall of Fame despite his lifetime ban for betting on the Reds, framed by retributive versus utilitarian theories of punishment. Aeon Skoble argues yes: betting on one's own team to win commits no fraud like throwing games, and Cooperstown honors baseball excellence, not moral perfection — the Hall already enshrines racists, adulterers, and cheats. Mark Hamilton answers no with the Dowd Report's evidence, Rule 21(d), and Giamatti's banishment statement: a managing gambler may sacrifice the season to settle tonight's debt, and reinstatement without remorse would declare the game's rules toothless.

A paired political-philosophy debate over Alex Rodriguez's $252 million contract. Albert Duncan defends the salary as the just outcome of market forces: stars like Bonds, McGwire, and Sosa maximize fan satisfaction, pack stadiums (600,000 extra Cardinals tickets in 1998), and generate hundreds of millions for local economies. Joel Shuman, a self-described socialist, replies with Alasdair MacIntyre's notion of baseball as a 'practice' whose intrinsic goods belong to a traditioned community of players, coaches, and fans: when market ideology alienates fans, unbalances competition, and prices out small markets, money has stopped serving the human activity it was meant to be part of.

A paired metaphysics debate on whether superstition helps performance. Steven Streeter argues yes: baseball's mystery-rich outcomes breed ritual (Sparky Anderson refusing to step on foul lines, Wade Boggs's chicken, Nomar Garciaparra's glove taps), whose invisible forces — like black holes — can be inferred from their measurable effects on attention, preparation, and focus, with William James's belief-makes-reality as the capstone. Neil Feit counters no: on the counterfactual account of helping, a player cured of superstition would perform the same since his athletic ability is untouched, routines that aid concentration need involve no magical belief, and the burden of proof lies with the believer.

A paired legal-philosophy debate on whether steroids should be banned. Michael McGrath argues yes from Kant: PED use cannot be universalized and 'the ends do not justify the means,' so the Ken Caminiti, Mark McGwire, and José Canseco confessions stain America's pastime, whose stars are role models and whose users risk devastating health effects — down to wrestler Davey Boy Smith's fatal steroid-related heart attack. Simon Eassom replies no by reframing drugs as Performance Enhancing Technologies: rules merely define the game, enhancers (unlike bat-cannons or netted catcher's gloves) do not de-skill baseball, and banning them because we dislike them is a matter of taste — of aesthetics, not ethics.

A paired aesthetics debate over the best baseball movie. Vincent Toscano picks The Natural: Robert Redford's Roy Hobbs enacts fall and redemption, Barry Levinson's halo-lit amber cinematography gives the film its mythic beauty, and its Reagan-era warmth answered America's post-sixties malaise. Larry Raful counters with It Happens Every Spring: the best baseball film lets the common man — Ray Milland's chemistry teacher armed with a wood-repelling mystery juice — dream himself into the Show, and he notes we cheer fictional cheating on screen while demanding that the real game stay pure.

A paired philosophy-of-education debate on whether baseball players were better role models then or now. Edward Sullivan answers 'then' from lived memory: Ted Williams's Korean War service and his 1966 Hall of Fame induction speech demanding Satchel Paige and Josh Gibson be enshrined, and Jackie Robinson enduring Jim Crow spring training under Branch Rickey's pact of 'guts enough not to fight back.' Graham Harman answers 'now,' turning Socrates's Apology complaint that his most dangerous accusers are those safely dead into a diagnosis of nostalgia: the past buried Ty Cobb's and Cap Anson's racism, the Black Sox, and Hal Chase, while today's game is more racially open, physically dedicated, and union-protected.

holes.name: Charles Darwin
holes.what: Originator of the theory of evolution by natural selection, whose own account of human development (cultural rather than genetic evolution in The Descent of Man) diverged sharply from the 'Social Darwinism' built on his name.
holes.why: Chapter 25 argues the Negro Leagues refuted Social Darwinism precisely by invoking Darwin's actual view that cultural, not genetic, development explains human achievement.

holes.name: Bushido (the Way of the Warrior)
holes.what: The Japanese samurai ethical code stressing loyalty, self-denial, austerity, relentless training, and honor.
holes.why: Chapter 29's central question is whether Japanese baseball is genuinely shaped by Bushido's resolve and 'training of death' or whether that is an over-generalization about Japanese culture.

holes.name: Games as Artificial Tests (lusory goals)
holes.what: The philosophy-of-sport view (associated with Bernard Suits) that games are rule-built artificial problems whose point is the mutual, appropriately difficult testing of skills.
holes.why: Chapter 34's verdict on the intentional walk rests entirely on whether walking Barry Bonds avoids the game's test or merely shifts it to other players.
